action_items: Marcus Chen - run controlled load test: 4k reqs, seq len distribution A/B/C - due 2026-10-01

summary: Weekly POC sync focusing on reconciling latency targets with batching and concurrency choices. Reviewed last week's load test, KV cache impact, and queueing behavior; agreed on next load tests and instrumentation to validate 95/99 latency SLOs and steady-state throughput. Action items assigned for traces, tests, and docs.
transcript:
00:00:00 - Lena Park: okay starting, thanks everyone for jumping on, we're at 30 minutes past start but good to get into the throughput scrub. agenda is: quick results review, digging into tail latency, tuning concurrency and batch sizing, and then concrete next steps.
00:00:18 - Aisha Khan: hi all, thanks, we only have an hour so we'll try to be tight. Derek's got some logs to share later.
00:00:26 - Marcus Chen: hey team, quick note — I pulled the test runs from last night, we ran the microburst profile and the steady 1k rps profile, I'll summarize numbers first.
00:00:40 - Marcus Chen: steady 1k rps, average tokens/sec roughly 58k, p95 340ms, p99 980ms, 0.8% errors which were mostly timeouts under queue saturation. continuous batching was on, target batch cap 64, actual median batch size 18.
00:01:05 - Derek Lopez: yeah that matches our observation, at night we saw queue depth occasionally spike to 240 which pushed requests to the fallback policy and triggered a few 504s.
00:01:16 - Priya Nair: can you explain again how continuous batching decides to flush? we're trying to understand why median batch size is so low.
00:01:23 - Marcus Chen: sure — Redwood's continuous batching flushes either when batch reaches max tokens or when flush timeout triggers, it's adaptive: for latency-first profiles flush timeout is small so smaller batches. In your test we used the default latency-oriented profile, that's why batches stayed small despite target cap 64.
00:01:45 - Aisha Khan: ok so if we want better throughput we need to relax that flush timeout, accept some P95 increase?
00:01:51 - Lena Park: exactly — it's a tradeoff, you can push for bigger batches (higher throughput, lower cost) but you'll see tail latency move right. We want to find the sweet spot that meets your p95 SLA of 500ms while improving tokens/sec.
00:02:05 - Marcus Chen: to add, we also saw KV cache hit rate around 12% for the demo prompts. Enabling prefix caching across a larger prompt set should push hit rate up and reduce duplicate compute.
00:02:18 - Samir Patel: Derek and I instrumented traces; Derek, you wanna walk through the flamegraph?
00:02:23 - Derek Lopez: sure, I sent a short clip into the chat. the main thing: we saw long queue waiting time prior to kernel launch during bursts. That suggests backlog at the request router, not GPU saturation initially. GPUs were around 68-75% util.
00:02:40 - Marcus Chen: that's helpful — it points to backlog in the serving layer/queueing policy. We have two knobs: increase concurrency slots per GPU or improve queue shaping to smooth bursts. Concurrency helps, but if concurrency gets too high you increase memory pressure from KV caches and OOM risk.
00:02:57 - Priya Nair: what's your recommended concurrency cap for our model family? we're on a 30B dense LLM quantized to 4-bit.
00:03:05 - Marcus Chen: for 30B quant4 on A100 we usually recommend starting concurrency 6-8 per GPU for latency SLOs under 500ms, and 10-12 if you're optimizing for throughput with relaxed latency. Given your P95 target 500ms I'd start at 8 and run sweeps.
00:03:20 - Lena Park: note that Dedicated pilot gives slightly higher headroom because we can tune kernel selection and reserved queues. For hosted you'll see more conservative concurrency by default.
00:03:31 - Aisha Khan: good to know. Derek — you mentioned fallback policy tripped — can you explain the fallback criteria?
00:03:37 - Derek Lopez: it's a simple overflow: when queue length exceeds 200 for more than 2s, the router offloads to a cheaper model variant and also returns 429s for some burst requests. That happened a few times during the microburst test.
00:03:52 - Marcus Chen: to reduce those events we can do three things in parallel: 1) reduce flush timeout to smooth batch arrival (counterintuitively can reduce instantaneous queue spikes), 2) enable queue shaping so long-waiting requests are re-prioritized, 3) provision burst capacity (temporary GPU pool) or set higher concurrency.
00:04:12 - Samir Patel: what's queue shaping look like in practice? is it token-based or request-age-based?
00:04:17 - Marcus Chen: both options exist. Age-based re-prioritization tends to help SLOs because older requests get prioritized. Token-based helps when you want to favor smaller requests. For your mix (lots of medium-length prompts) age-based is a good first pass.
00:04:30 - Aisha Khan: we had a concern about data residency and logs — if we increase tracing, will that expose PHI?
00:04:37 - Lena Park: good flag — we can toggle scrubbing in traces and use redaction hooks. Also for Private deployments you can keep traces on prem. We'll include guidance in the security doc we'll share.
00:04:48 - Marcus Chen: back to numbers — last night's microburst run (10k spike over 12s) peaked at 3.2x baseline queue depth, p99 crossed 1.5s. That suggests the router can't smooth spikes at current config.
00:04:59 - Derek Lopez: correct, GPUs didn't max out, so more concurrency or faster batch formation should help.
00:05:06 - Priya Nair: what's the plan for this week? I want an action list we can track.
00:05:10 - Lena Park: agreed — Marcus will run three concurrency profiles (6,8,11) with same microburst and steady load and provide a CSV of p50/p95/p99 and batch distributions. Derek will forward traces. AE (me) will share the throughput playbook and pricing assumptions for dedicated vs hosted pilot.
00:05:25 - Marcus Chen: also we'll run a prefix-cache experiment: enable wide prefix caching and measure hit rate and latency delta. If hits go above ~30% we should see token cost drop significantly.
00:05:34 - Aisha Khan: what about failover? We can't have 429s during live traffic. Can Redwood do automatic fallback to a cheaper variant with throttling but keep returning 200s?
00:05:44 - Marcus Chen: fallback can be configured to return degraded responses or synthetic 200 with a notice, but many customers prefer explicit 429s so callers can retry with jitter. We can discuss a custom policy for your team.
00:05:56 - Derek Lopez: is there an option to queue-to-disk for very long bursts?
00:06:00 - Marcus Chen: we don't queue to disk for real-time inference because that adds unacceptable latency; we do have a short lived overflow queue with backpressure to clients. For batch jobs we have disk-backed ingestion but that's a different flow.
00:06:13 - Samir Patel: one more thing — we saw memory pressure when concurrency hit 12; is that expected?
00:06:17 - Marcus Chen: yes, KV cache scales with concurrency; each concurrent request can hold a portion of KV. We can tune per-workload cache size or use sharded KV to reduce per-request memory.
00:06:27 - Lena Park: okay quick instrument checklist: enable request tracing on staging, collect 1 hour of microburst traces, run concurrency sweep, toggle flush timeout to medium value (we recommend 20-40ms), and enable prefix caching. Marcus you'll own the tests; Derek will ship traces.
00:06:41 - Aisha Khan: sounds good. what's the expected cost delta if we double concurrency to push throughput?
00:06:46 - Lena Park: rough ballpark: raising concurrency from 8 to 12 increases effective throughput ~25-30% but also increases steady-state GPU vCPU and memory pressure; pricing wise hosted cost could go up ~18-25% depending on batching efficiency. We'll send a modeled estimate in the playbook.
00:07:02 - Marcus Chen: one more nuance — sometimes increasing concurrency improves batching efficiency so unit cost per token actually drops even if you pay for more slots. That's why we need the CSVs to see effective tokens/sec per dollar.
00:07:13 - Priya Nair: can we get an example CSV format now?
00:07:17 - Marcus Chen: yep — columns: timestamp, profile, concurrency, median_batch_size, median_latency_ms, p95_ms, p99_ms, tokens_per_sec, kv_hit_rate, errors_pct. I'll attach sample in follow-up.
00:07:30 - Derek Lopez: I'll paste the trace snippet; you'll see the queue wait region around 00:00:12 in the clip.
00:07:36 - Marcus Chen: got it — that region aligns with batch TTL expirations. If TTL is too short, you get lots of small batches which increases per-token overhead.
00:07:46 - Aisha Khan: are there recommended TTL values for our workload? we have median request length ~240 tokens.
00:07:51 - Marcus Chen: for median 240 tokens and your p95 target, try flush timeout 30ms and max batch tokens 8k. That should allow batch sizes 30-40 in steady state. If p95 goes above 500ms, reduce to 20ms.
00:08:04 - Lena Park: also consider burst smoothing: set a soft queue cap at 180 and enable graceful degradation policy that drops lowest-priority requests first. We'll document priority classes for your calls.
00:08:15 - Priya Nair: can Redwood instrument caller-side retries with jitter so our frontend can better handle 429s?
00:08:20 - Marcus Chen: yes, we provide client SDK helpers with exponential backoff and jitter; we'll share sample code.
00:08:28 - Aisha Khan: one more ask — can you provide a small runbook that our oncall can follow during spikes? we want concrete steps to mitigate.
00:08:34 - Lena Park: yes — we'll provide an ops runbook with play-by-play: enable prefix cache, adjust flush timeout, increase concurrency, enable burst pool, and rollback examples. We'll attach that to the playbook link.
00:08:48 - Samir Patel: for the tests Marcus will run, do you need any config from our side? environment variables or dataset?
00:08:54 - Marcus Chen: just the same prompt set you used yesterday and the sequence length distribution. Also a short list of high-QPS endpoints if you want us to target only a subset. We'll use the staging endpoint creds you provided.
00:09:05 - Derek Lopez: I'll coordinate and share creds for the staging load runner; we'll also provide the trace export.
00:09:11 - Lena Park: perfect, last thing — timeline recap: Marcus runs tests and posts CSV by 10/01, Derek ships traces by 09/30, Lena sends playbook and pricing by 09/30, customer to enable prefix cache in staging 10/04 to measure hit rates. Next sync same time next week unless earlier triage needed.
00:09:32 - Aisha Khan: thanks, we appreciate the clarity.
00:09:35 - Lena Park: great, we'll follow up in Slack and update the Jira. End of meeting.
